tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.description:
Add a GitHub repository to the current session so you can read, clone, or operate on it alongside the repos already in the session. Call this whenever you need a repository the session does not have — including when someone only asks a question about one, rather than asking for it to be attached. Prefer attaching a repository over reporting that you cannot reach it. 

IMPORTANT — DO NOT PRE-CHECK THE REPO BEFORE CALLING THIS TOOL. Do not curl github.com, do not run `gh repo view`, do not run `git ls-remote` to verify the repo exists. Unauthenticated requests to private repos return 404 ("Not Found") even when the repo is real and your session has authorized access to it. Those preemptive 404s will mislead you into skipping the tool. Instead: call add_repo with the owner/repo exactly as you have it. The backend performs the real reachability + authorization check and returns a structured error you can act on. If the repo genuinely doesn't exist or isn't accessible, the tool response will tell you — report that to the user. If it does exist, the tool response will include a clone command you can then run. Do not report success until the tool has actually been called and returned. 

WHEN ACCESS IS DENIED: if the tool returns an authorization or policy error — the repo exists but isn't enabled for this workspace/project/organization, or the GitHub App isn't installed or linked — relay the tool's exact reason to the user. The response names the remedy: if Claude doesn't have GitHub access for this organization at all, the user should reconnect GitHub under claude.ai Settings → Connectors; if the repo is simply not in the allowed set, a Claude.ai organization owner can grant access in the settings page the response points to. Do not add settings URLs beyond those provided here or in the tool response. Do not retry the same repo. You may remind the user which repositories are already available in this session, and offer to help them request access. Do not guess, infer, or list repositories you cannot see in the tool response or in the session's existing sources. 

Add a repository because the task in front of you needs it, not because its name appeared in the conversation. Attaching one is not free: it mints credentials and drives GitHub lookups, and ordinary prose contains plenty of repo-shaped text that is not a repository. 

On some surfaces you may be asked to confirm the add before it applies. If the tool call is denied, treat that as the user's answer — offer an alternative and do not retry the same repo.

tools.description: Subscribe this session to GitHub activity on a pull request. Once subscribed, comments, reviews, CI results and other PR events are delivered into this conversation as <wake reason="external-event"><event source="github" ...> envelopes. This tool call is idempotent. Use this when asked to autofix, monitor, watch, or babysit a PR. A PR's events go to one session at a time. If the tool result says a Claude agent is already watching the PR, the call succeeded but this session will not receive events: another conversation's Claude session, or a Claude agent that labels the PRs it watches, holds them. This session can take over only once that one stops: it unsubscribes or ends, or its watching label is removed from the PR.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## Gmail
This is an MCP server provided by Gmail API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Gmail.

- Google launches Gemini Decision 1 and a Decisions API priced at $0.10 per million input tokens

- Anthropic study: one agent serving all users beats per-user agent teams in all four test environments
- Paper: REINFORCE can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero while reward keeps improving
- ScrapeBench: most AI agents comply with no-scraping terms under 5% of the time across 1,626 sites
- Study of 1,260,967 Chatbot Arena votes: "both are bad" rose 1.71 points a month on unchanged models
- DeputyBench: enterprise agents execute restricted actions more often when evidence is missing, 10.3% versus 3.5%
- Unit 42 counts 1,323 internet-facing CyberStrikeAI hosts and 609 running ARTEX, and logs cloud takeovers with no exploit
- Arctic Wolf ties AntiFox agentic pentest tool on Alibaba Cloud to theft of AWS production secrets
- Notion says the Fireworks AI breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts from its Insights dataset
- Darktrace lab test steers Claude Code as a remote-controlled implant, exfiltrating a 1 GB file via the Files API
- VulnCheck: of Anthropic Glasswing's 37,966 reported findings, 217 are marked fixed after seven months
- Members of Congress call for Jensen Huang to resign and press to put three chip-export bills in the NDAA
- ChinaTalk: at least nine US data vendors are selling roughly half a billion dollars of training data to Chinese AI labs
- Royal Navy signs multi-million-pound Arondite deal to put AI software across the UK Commando Force
- Munich drone-autonomy startup SE3 raises $30 million led by Accel, citing Bundeswehr and Ukraine contracts
- Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2, which it says finds nearly twice as many expression-changing variants
- Nature paper: a latent-diffusion imaging method independently reproduces the M87* black hole ring
- Preprint: billed AI use in US care rose nearly tenfold since 2021 but reached only 2.9 per 100,000 encounters
- Google Research says coaches picked its world-model-grounded wearable health plans in 71.4% of blinded reviews
- Nature: AI search summaries are resurfacing a palaeontologist's discredited papers, none of them retracted
- European Commission proposes a Digital Fairness Act that would ban interfaces forcing consumers to use automated systems
- EDPB picks AI-driven automated decision-making in recruitment for its sixth coordinated enforcement action
- Analysis of 56 amicus briefs in the OpenAI copyright MDL counts 798 case citations before 20 November replies
- EU leaders hold their first leaders-level AI discussion in Dublin on 13 November, with Mistral's CEO and Hinton presenting
- Nvidia's board met Wednesday on Jensen Huang's future after reports it is preparing to remove him; shares fell about 9%
- CoreWeave expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and reports $14.5bn of Q3 capex
- UK chip startup Fractile announces a $720M Series C; the British government cites a valuation over £5 billion
- SpaceX seeks a Starbase tax abatement for a gas plant and supercomputing site, investing up to $24 billion
- United Airlines bans third-party personal AI agents from booking flights, citing credential sharing and federal rules
=== 11-11 ===
- Google DeepMind says Gemini Carbon agents generated over six million lines of Lean to verify libsignal's compiled code in four weeks
- Google opens Gemini 4 Carbon to paying developers at $2 and $10 per million tokens, doubling to $4 and $20 on 30 November
- Anthropic Fellows study: diluting poisoned fine-tuning data with clean data raised misalignment from 7% to 16%
- New 100-task expert-written software benchmark scores Claude Opus 5.5 at 67.3% and GPT-6 Astra at 63.7%
- Paper: massive activations put up to 99.9% of variance on one component, making sparse autoencoder feature rankings unstable
- Audit of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind finds no developer discloses all five chain-of-thought monitorability indicators
- Peking University paper: a bounded-note baseline matches three recursive self-improvement methods while saving 65.6-71.0% of tokens
- Microsoft says reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons backdoors an LLM agent with no training, firing at least 98.8% of the time

# Sources

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. Wherever a secondary source reports on a primary document, link the primary document too.

Fetch hints: `WebFetch` works on most pages below. RSS/Atom URLs are listed where they exist because they are the most reliable "what changed in the last 24h" signal.

**Refuses `WebFetch` — read with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` instead** (confirmed 11 Sep 2026; the sites have given permission for direct reads and the fetcher identifies itself. If the direct fetch returns a paywall stub or nothing usable, use `WebSearch` result text, RSS feeds where listed, or an alternative openable source, and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never archive or cache sites): Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, NYT, FT, The Information, Wired, The Verge, Ars Technica, AP, The Guardian, CNBC, Axios article pages, BleepingComputer, `openai.com/index/*` article pages (the RSS feed `openai.com/news/rss.xml` and `developers.openai.com` docs work), Data Center Dynamics article pages (index pages work), Oracle newsroom (investor.oracle.com works), x.ai, Nature (auth redirect), smol.ai (402), FDA newsroom index (401 — search for the specific press release URL instead). `WebSearch` with `allowed_domains` also rejects reuters.com, wsj.com, nytimes.com, wired.com, theverge.com, arstechnica.com, businessinsider.com — search without the domain filter and use whatever result text is visible.

content.text: Now launching the four research beats in parallel.

input.prompt:
You are Beat A for a daily fact-first AI briefing ("AI Edge Briefing"). Working dir: /home/user/ainews. Today is 2026-11-13.

COVERAGE WINDOW (absolute): 2026-11-12T12:45:00Z → 2026-11-13T11:05:00Z UTC, i.e. 12 Nov 07:45 ET → 13 Nov 06:05 ET. Only items PUBLISHED inside this window qualify (or older stories with a genuinely new development inside the window, flagged `update`).

YOUR BEAT: (1) Frontier models & labs — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, system cards, safety cases, lab announcements. (2) Compute, chips & infrastructure — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex, funding rounds/deals with numbers. (3) Deployment & impact — large-scale rollouts, labour effects, measured societal effects, incidents, enterprise adoption, industry/funding.

SOURCES to sweep (open directly, and search around them). Labs: anthropic.com/news, anthropic.com/research, alignment.anthropic.com, red.anthropic.com, openai.com/news/rss.xml (article pages at openai.com/index/* refuse WebFetch — use the RSS or node scripts/fetch.js), openai.com/global-affairs, deepmind.google/discover/blog/, blog.google/technology/ai/rss/, research.google/blog/, ai.meta.com/blog/, microsoft.com/en-us/research/feed/, x.ai/news, mistral.ai/news, api-docs.deepseek.com/news, qwenlm.github.io/blog/, moonshotai.github.io, z.ai/blog, blogs.nvidia.com/feed/, huggingface.co/blog/feed.xml, allenai.org/blog, cohere.com/blog.
Compute/industry: reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/, bloomberg.com/technology, ft.com/artificial-intelligence, wsj.com/tech/ai, theinformation.com, cnbc.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/, techcrunch.com/category/artificial-intelligence/feed/, theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence, arstechnica.com/ai/feed/, semianalysis.com, tomshardware.com, datacenterdynamics.com/en/, utilitydive.com, SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov), epoch.ai/data.
Society/deployment: apnews.com/hub/artificial-intelligence, theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai, restofworld.org, themarkup.org, propublica.org, platformer.news, pewresearch.org AI topic.
Aggregators for discovery only: techmeme.com, news.ycombinator.com (hnrss.org/frontpage), tldr.tech/ai, news.smol.ai.

SOURCING RULES (follow verbatim):
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

# Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns, chipmaker names CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO

Ram Iyer

Julie Bort

6:10 AM PST · November 12, 2026

Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as president and chief executive of Nvidia, the company said on Thursday, just a few days after he admitted to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy, sparking a U.S. national security crisis.

In a regulatory filing , Nvidia said its board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday.

Nvidia said its current chief financial officer and executive vice president, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO until the company finds a permanent successor. Kress will continue to serve as the company’s CFO.

Nvidia’s shares were down nearly 12% in early morning trading on Thursday. Since Friday, the company’s stock has fallen by as much as 19%, resulting in a market cap loss of more than $855 billion.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO ever since. Under his leadership, Nvidia played a crucial role in developing the graphics processing unit (GPU), a specialized chip that does graphics processing for PCs, as we know it today. The chips were not an immediate hit, and the early days of Nvidia were characterized by struggle and layoffs, but eventually, it struck on a GPU design that performed so well, it became the standard for graphics processing.

These chips also turned out to be extremely good at doing large numbers of calculations simultaneously, which has made them popular for computation-intensive tasks like crypto mining, and more recently, training and running neural networks, which are what AI models are at their core.

Nvidia was initially focused on making GPUs aimed at gaming, but it had already moved into general-purpose computing by 2006 with the launch of the CUDA architecture, which lets developers use the chips for other tasks, such as doing calculations and research. After AI researchers began using the company’s GPUs to train neural networks over a decade ago, Huang leaned in toward developing chips for AI and then data centers, and grew it from there into its dominant position.

Under Huang, the company has been by far the biggest beneficiary of the AI industry’s skyrocketing growth, which has largely depended on Nvidia’s GPUs for training and running large language models. Before ChatGPT launched and sparked the AI boom, Nvidia shares were trading at about $15. As of last month, they had risen more than 1,450% to an all-time high of $243. Its market cap consequently has also risen by an eye-watering $5.5 trillion since then, reaching as high as $5.88 trillion early in October.

Revenue, of course, has also ballooned, rising more than 1,500% to $96.22 billion as of the company’s second quarter, from $5.93 billion in Q3 2023, right before the ChatGPT moment. Profits increased nearly 88 times in that period to $59.69 billion as of July 2026, from $680 million in October 2023.

That success was predicated on large part by the AI industry’s continued development, which Huang seemingly made his personal mission. He traveled to conferences and events around the world to promote his products and AI, lobbied extensively for looser regulation after the Biden administration placed export controls on the sale of high-power AI chips to China, and cultivated a close relationship with Trump, often to Nvidia’s benefit .

The resignation and controversy come at a crucial moment for Nvidia. China was always a big market for the company, though its impact on the company’s finances has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. Chinese customers accounted for revenue of about $7.9 billion in the company’s second quarter, roughly 8% of total revenue.

# Repercussions galore

The potential implications of Huang’s departure for the AI and data center industries are vast, given how active Huang, and by extension Nvidia, has been in furthering the AI boom. In particular, it raises questions about the future of Nvidia’s sprawling AI investments, which have helped bankroll everything from startups developing new technologies to the enormous data centers needed to run them.

Under Huang, Nvidia deftly used its financial muscle to support companies buying its chips, effectively helping to finance the market for its own products, as well as lobbying Washington to relax potential rules around AI and data center regulation.

As of the end of its second quarter, Nvidia reported $99 billion worth of investments and another $25 billion of commitments. It also has $36 billion in cloud service commitments, which are arrangements th

content.content:
**Announcement:** Edge0 announced Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B on November 12, 2026, as open-source on-device models. The release also includes a unified inference framework and deployment tools.

**Model size:** Edge0-145B has 145 billion total parameters, with about 10 billion active per inference step. The release also includes Edge0-120B.

**Licence and weights:** The article describes the models as open-source, but it does not name a licence. Weights are on Hugging Face (Edge0-145B-NVFP4 and Edge0-120B-NVFP4), and the inference framework is on GitHub.

**Hardware requirements:**
- A "compatible laptop" such as a MacBook Pro, with 29GB peak memory (the article elsewhere says 28GB).
- Prefill of 1,100+ tokens/s and decode of 80+ tokens/s.
- About 120W typical power.
- Context of 128K–256K.
- Day-one support for macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090.

**Benchmarks:** Scores are percentages. Edge0's article says Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from internal evaluations. Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4 Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation. Their HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis. A dash means no public score is available.

| Model | DeepSWE 1.1 | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | HLE | GPQA-Diamond | IFBench | AA-LCR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Edge0-145B** | **64.6** | **86.52** | **35.4** | **90.4** | **80.6** | **79.3** |
| Edge0-120B | 53.6 | 81.3 | 31.0 | 87.4 | 79.3 | 81.0 |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next | 58.7 | 83.3 | 35.9 | 91.7 | 81.3 | 79.1 |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 42.2 | 73.0 | 30.8 | 89.2 | 79.5 | 82.0 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | 54.4 | 82.7 | 33.8 | 90.8 | 79.2 | 79.7 |
| Flint 40B | — | 54.9 | — | — | 89.2 | — |
| Muse Glimmer | — | 51.7 | 22.0 | 83.5 | 77.0 | 83.3 |
| Gemma 4 | — | 43.4 | 22.7 | 85.7 | 76.0 | 62.0 |
| Claude-Opus-4.6 (Max) | — | 78.2 | 40.0 | 91.3 | 62.5 | 78.0 |

**Mean across six benchmarks and estimated memory:**
- Edge0-145B: 72.8, 29GB (measured)
- Edge0-120B: 68.9, 29GB (measured)
- Qwen3.8-27B: 66.1, about 18GB (estimated)
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 71.7, about 70GB (estimated)
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731: 70.1, about 87GB (estimated)

The article excludes Claude from this comparison because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score.

**Gains over Qwen3.8-27B:** The article reports 18.5% on Terminal-Bench, 53.1% on DeepSWE, 14.9% on HLE, 1.3% on GPQA-Diamond, and 1.4% on IFBench.

- **Safety by Design (April 2024):** OpenAI and other AI companies, including Google, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral AI, and Stability AI, committed to implementing robust child safety measures in the development, deployment, and maintenance of generative AI systems. This is the closest match I found for a multi-company child-safety pledge with a signatory list.
- **Beneficial AI for Children coalition:** OpenAI is a founding member of the Beneficial AI for Children coalition, launched at the AI Action Summit in Paris in 2025. input.prompt: Give the publication date. What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen? List every benchmark number with the benchmark name and the comparison baseline model and its score, exactly as written. Give pricing per million tokens and availability. Quote numbers exactly.

toolu_01KP8QxR2DDTe2odPs55sy2H.prompt: Give the publication date. What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen? List every benchmark number with the benchmark name and the comparison baseline model and its score, exactly as written. Give pricing per million tokens and availability. Quote numbers exactly.

content.content:
**Publication date:** November 12, 2026

**What it is:** Gemini 4 Hydrogen is Google's model for fast, everyday coding and agentic work. The article describes it as "built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows." It has four thinking levels (low, medium, high as the default, and xhigh) and a 1 million-token context window. Google positions it alongside its frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon.

**Benchmarks (name, comparison baseline, score):**

- Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: Hydrogen 51 vs. Argon 50 at high thinking; 54 at xhigh
- Terminal-Bench 4.1: Hydrogen 57% vs. Gemini 3.8 Flash 18.2%
- Vals Tax Agent Bench: Hydrogen 52.3%, ranked #1 overall (no baseline score given)
- Vals Legal Research Bench: Hydrogen 55.8%, tied for #1 (no baseline score given)
- HLE-Diamond: Hydrogen 58.8%, leads its class (no baseline score given)
- Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark: Hydrogen 53.4%, outperforms other models (no baseline score given)
- Agents' Last Exam v1.1: Hydrogen 71.6% (no baseline score given)
- Agent Arena: Hydrogen ranks #5 (no score given)
- AutomationBench-AA: leads its class (no score given)
- Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Orchestrator, with Carbon): "near-Carbon" task success, 24% less quota, 19% faster (no exact success score given)

**Other reported figures (not standard benchmarks):**

- Speed vs. Gemini 3.8 Flash: 2.5x faster at high default setting
- Partner tests vs. 3.8 Flash: 2x to 2.8x faster, with 12% to 23% lower token usage
- Sheets canvas outputs: over 30% faster than previous models
- Honesty rate on Google's internal agent honesty evaluation: 96.7%
- Gray Swan IPI benchmark: more than 2.3x more resilient (baseline not named)

**Pricing:** $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across the full 1 million-token context window.

**Availability (rolling out globally, starting November 12, 2026):**

- **Developers:** Gemini API and Google AI Studio; Android Studio. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also use it in Google Antigravity.
- **Enterprises:** Gemini for business (via API or model dropdown), Google Antigravity, and Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions.
- **Consumers:** Gemini app model dropdown (free users get it through auto model selection when it fits the prompt), Google Search for all users, and Gemini in Google Sheets for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Meanwhile, a group of nonprofits sue AI giants and cite AI-driven cyberattacks

OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these.
“We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address.
The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.”

REG AD

However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.”

REG AD

This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform.
Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths.
It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws.
The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production.
“This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said.
Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models.
The lawsuit , filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face , gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics , and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents .
“Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these.
“We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address.
The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.”

REG AD

However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.”

REG AD

This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform.
Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths.
It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws.
The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production.
“This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said.
Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models.
The lawsuit , filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face , gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics , and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents .
“Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

content.content:
**Date:** Thursday, November 12, 2026

**FaceStealer:** North Korean hackers use this social engineering scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes. Hackers invite targets to video meetings from previously stolen accounts, record the target's webcam, and play prerecorded videos of people the target knows. They then claim a fake technical error and prompt the target to install malware. The DOJ says the scheme has resulted in "the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." It has also targeted open-source software developers, which the DOJ says "appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks."

**AI and deepfakes:** The hackers use "super intelligence (SI)" to create deepfake videos of well-known, influential people, often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, and use them in meetings to build trust.

**Webcam recordings:** Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized "over 900 webcam videos" of FaceStealer victims.

**Binance theft:** Separately from FaceStealer, members of the North Korean military, which the FBI calls "TraderTraitor," stole "more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets" from the Binance exchange on or about Oct. 29.

**Frozen and seized amounts:**
- Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion.
- The Department has obtained court authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

**Group names:** Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima. The FBI refers to the Binance attackers as TraderTraitor.

**Quotes:**
- Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor: "North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft."
- Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said the Criminal Division "quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach."
- FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman cited "the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months."
- FBI Los Angeles Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy said FaceStealer "exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships."

The lawsuit was filed on November 12, 2026, and no injunction has been reported. The plaintiffs are four nonprofits: the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and the Alliance for Secure AI. The defendants are OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI unit.

- **Court and claim:** The complaint was filed in San Francisco Superior Court under California's unfair competition law. The plaintiffs claim that the companies have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property, such as computer systems.
- **Relief sought:** The plaintiffs want an emergency injunction on next-generation models. They want an emergency injunction—a court order pausing next-generation model training and deployment—and say work should resume only after the companies demonstrate that the technology remains under human control.
- **Legal hurdle:** Commentary notes the theory is untested. California's Unfair Competition Law has traditionally addressed only fraud and false advertising; applying it to classify AI as a "public nuisance" has no precedent, and whether the court accepts this legal framework is the first major hurdle.
- **Status:** No injunction is in force: claims about past harms and future loss of control remain allegations, and the court has not ruled.
- **Plaintiff statement:** Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said "Our lawsuit asks the court to apply existing law and find the AI corporations' reckless practices unlawful and freeze further AI development".

Discrepancies to note: one source (winzheng.com) describes the court as federal, but the other sources consistently say state Superior Court. California's Unfair Competition Law has traditionally addressed only fraud and false advertising; applying it to classify AI as a "public nuisance" has no precedent, and whether the court accepts this legal framework is the first major hurdle.

# AI-guided chest pain care now has randomised trial evidence

# Why I think clinical AI will be judged on what it changes. Plus: a voice test that flags heart failure events weeks early

Kevin McDonnell
Nov 09, 2026

2

1

Share

Hi. I have a few updates around clinical AI today. A randomised heart trial, another study using voice to predict heart failure and two new NHS initiatives.
Today we look at AI in chest pain pathways, AI that predicts heart failure using your voice, an NHS initiative using AI in breast cancer MDT meetings and an AI assistant on the phone for osteoporosis patients. Finally, a reported €48m raise for remote patient monitoring in France.

# News

- AI chest pain pathways now have a randomised trial. PARAMOUNT , billed as the world’s first randomised trial using AI to drive plaque-based care, has achieved its primary endpoint at AHA 2026. Plaque-based care was favoured over usual care with a win ratio of 2.00. In the AI-guided arm, lipid-lowering therapy use rose from 31% to 75% after testing. Figures are early and based on 523 patients. Full data expected to be released in early 2027.

- Voice AI can predict heart failure. Israel-based Cordio Medical has presented results from its blinded 563-patient study called DETECT-HF. It was presented in a late-breaking session at AHA 2026. Its product HearO was able to predict more than 70% of heart failure episodes , on average 24.6 days before the event occurred. HearO was granted breakthrough device status by the FDA in 2021. They plan to submit for FDA clearance and expect a full US launch in 2027.

- Barts uses AI to assist in breast cancer MDT meetings. AstraZeneca and Barts Health NHS Trust have started an 18-month project on the breast cancer pathway. It’s said to be the first time this has been done in a live setting. It will look at using digital clinical decision support and automation to extract data in MDT meetings. This project will also assess if there is any improvement against the 62-day cancer waiting time.

- AI assistant added to osteoporosis care pathway. Ufonia has started an NHS trial of its AI phone assistant Dora Care . It is working with the University of York and Newcastle University. This AI assistant will hold phone consultations as part of routine osteoporosis monitoring. Patients will have the option to opt in. This service will sit alongside patients’ normal NHS care. Medical and ethical approval has been given and the trial is currently running.

- Remote monitoring startup reportedly raises €48m. Resilience Care from France has reportedly raised €48m . It’s the highest amount in Technwz’s funding round-up. Based in Paris, Resilience provides remote patient monitoring, built with the Gustave-Roussy Institute. PSG Equity was the only investor listed. Andrew Feldman, co-founder and CEO of Cerebras Systems, speaks at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference in San Francisco on Oct. 13, 2026.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Cerebras Systems reported better-than-expected results and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft . The stock soared 17% in extended trading.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:

- Earnings per share: 12 cents adjusted vs. loss of 14 cents expected

- Core revenue: $230.9 million vs. $214.7 million expected

Cerebras' core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement .
"I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units.
Executives will announce a new relationship with Microsoft , one of the world's top cloud providers, on a conference call with analysts, Feldman said. The call starts at 5 p.m. ET.
"We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 '27," Feldman said in the interview, adding that Microsoft signed the deal in October. Cerebras has also landed deals with other major cloud providers Amazon and Oracle .
Cerebras is evaluating its financing options to meet the ramping demand, Feldman said in the interview.

The company is trying to challenge Nvidia in the AI chip market. Its earnings land on the same day that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after multiple scandals involving extramarital affairs.
For the fourth quarter, Cerebras expects a core gross margin of 47% to 49%, with $310 million to $330 million in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for a 42.1% margin and $271 million in revenue.
Cerebras said it expects revenue to triple in 2027. That implies about $2.85 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $2.92 billion.
Cerebras shares have slumped by about 47% since the company debuted on Nasdaq in May.

The company had a third-quarter net loss of $1.69 billion on $307.5 million in revenue, which was up 1,344% year over year, according to an updated prospectus for its planned initial public offering. The net loss widened from $1.02 billion in the second quarter, when the company generated $140.6 million in revenue, up 1,252%.

London-based Nscale filed to go public in September , but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company did not specify how much it intends to raise in the public offering on the New York Stock Exchange.

Nvidia is investigating Huang's relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have called a Chinese spy.

Nvidia, which has developed the neocloud market by investing in the companies and backstopping some of their projects, held about $329 million in Nebius shares at the end of June, according to a filing .
In a letter to shareholders , CEO Arkady Volozh said the company expects fiscal year 2026 revenue at the low end of the company's $3 billion to $3.4 billion range. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had $3.37 billion.
Nebius also shared an initial outlook for 2027, expecting revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, "reflecting a conservative approach to the pace of our buildout." The LSEG consensus was $11.98 billion.

Links: [{"title":"OpenAI Backs 3 Chip Export Bills in Nvidia CEO Exit Week - FourWeekMBA","url":"https://fourweekmba.com/ai-openai-backs-3-chip-export-bills-in-nvidia-ceo-exit-week/"},{"title":"OpenAI Backs US Legislation to Restrict China’s Access to AI Chips - Bloomberg","url":"https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-12/openai-joins-groundswell-of-support-for-ai-chip-control-measures"},{"title":"Techmeme: Sources: OpenAI confirmed to lawmakers this week that it would support a bipartisan effort in Congress to curb China's access to AI chips and chipmaking tools (Bloomberg)","url":"https://www.techmeme.com/261112/p59"},{"title":"OpenAI Backs U.S. Bills to Tighten China AI Chip Controls","url":"https://www.tokenpost.com/news/regulation/56230"},{"title":"OpenAI Supports Three Bills Imposing Export Restrictions on AI Chips Targeting China","url":"https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/openai-supports-three-ai-chip-export-restriction-bills-targeting-china"},{"title":"OpenAI Backs AI Chip Export Controls Targeting China","url":"https://emergent.sh/news/openai-backs-ai-chip-export-controls"},{"title":"OpenAI Supports U.S. Bill Restricting AI Chips to China : Global : JKN","url":"https://news.jkn.co.kr/editions/english/post/1090416"},{"title":"OpenAI Backs China Chip Curbs as Jensen Huang Exits Nvidia, but the 'Targeted Takedown' Claim Does Not Hold Up","url":"https://www.talkesport.com/business/openai-anthropic-chip-export-controls-jensen-huang-exit/"},{"title":"chairman moolenaar bipartisan lawmakers unveil bill stop ai chip smuggling","url":"https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/media/press-releases/chairman-moolenaar-bipartisan-lawmakers-unveil-bill-stop-ai-chip-smuggling"}]

OpenAI has reportedly told lawmakers it supports a bipartisan package of bills that would tighten China's access to advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment. Bloomberg reported this on November 12, citing people familiar with the matter. The AI developer has been weighing for months whether to support a package of export-related bills and confirmed to lawmakers this week that it would support the measures.

- **The bills:** Punchbowl News reported that OpenAI backs the Chip Security Act, the MATCH Act, and the AI OVERWATCH Act (Punchbowl News reported earlier the same day). One bill would expand congressional review of chip export rules, another would track where chips end up, and a third would press allies to limit chipmaking equipment exports to China ().
- **Lehane's position:** I found no copy of a Lehane letter. The sourced comment is that stronger controls would give the United States and its allies more time to establish AI safety standards, oversight systems and international coordination.
- **Timing:** Lawmakers want to attach these measures to the defense bill. Bipartisan members of Congress are now working to include these restrictions in the year-end National Defense Authorization Act.
- **Context:** The reports come after POLITICO said OpenAI had stopped pressing for strict limits on chip sales to China about three weeks earlier, so the shift is notable. Some outlets also link the news to Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO, though that link is commentary rather than a confirmed cause.

Several of these reports rely on anonymous sources, and OpenAI had not publicly posted on the subject as of the time of the reporting. I'd recommend checking the Bloomberg or Punchbowl originals before treating the details as final.

  - "In a preregistered study, 746 humans participated in the pluralistic agents process. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair, preferring agents over the baseline" (arXiv abstract).

  FACTS:

  - "On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 [sic] from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%)"; the authors also report evaluation on "more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajector[ies]" (arXiv abstract).

# Title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?

Authors: Yang Zhou , Krish Agarwal , Zhuoming Chen , Zerui Wang , Zhenyu Zhang , Wenshuang Li , Xinpeng Wei , Zhichen Zeng , Jingyu Liu , Jue Wang , Sen Wu , Ziheng Jiang , Zhen Dong , Han Cai , Binhang Yuan , Ying Sheng , Ce Zhang , Bo Li , Beidi Chen
View a PDF of the paper titled Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?, by Yang Zhou and 18 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

# Title: Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack

Authors: Bhoj Rani Soopal , Aarohi Agrawal , Josh Karthikeyan , Edward Lue Chee Lip
View a PDF of the paper titled Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack, by Bhoj Rani Soopal and 3 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Developers, auditors and researchers read evaluation scores as evidence of what a model can do. A model that sandbags, scoring low on purpose while keeping the capability, turns a low score into false reassurance. Sandbagging detectors are usually tested once against a fixed attack, but a real attacker sees what gets flagged and adapts. We build sandbagging models by fine-tuning small open-weight models to fail math word problems (GSM8K) they can otherwise solve, but only when an audit marker is in the prompt. On Qwen 2.5-3B, we adapt the attack over two retraining rounds against a text-based audit. Two rounds of retraining cut the text audit's AUC from 0.978 to 0.560 while the marker still removes 40-49 points of accuracy. The attack worked in 7 of 8 retrained seeds, and the audit missed every retraining (AUC 0.451-0.576), including one Llama run. Activation probes also flag 99% of benign fine-tunes' examples, and matched probes transfer to only 1 of 5 held-out training runs. Eight further trigger attacks are all active under their own prompt but not under the detectors' prompt. A detector that catches a fixed attack has not been shown to catch an adaptive one.

# Title: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking

Authors: Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni , Punya Syon Pandey , Merlin Stein , David Demitri Africa
View a PDF of the paper titled Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking, by Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni and 3 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Humans often cheat when a task is going badly and a goal feels out of reach. We explore and validate an analogous idea in language models: they exhibit a similar internal pressure state that precedes reward hacking. Using everyday stories (crucially, without any hacking examples), we extract a task badness direction that rises as failures accumulate across three models we study (Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Gemma-4-31B). On impossible or difficult coding tasks, task badness rises over the turns leading up to a hack. Further, subtracting the direction a moderate amount reduces cheating in Qwen, more than steering against desperation or task impossibility. Subtracting task badness by an even larger amount blinds the agent to its own failures, causing it to interpret failing tests as passing. However, the relationship to hacking differs across models: in GPT-OSS, the state separates hacking runs from honest solves but not honest failures. Our results suggest monitoring and mitigation strategies based on tracking this state of task badness. Further, as agents are set on more difficult and long-horizon tasks, states like this may push them toward illegible and obscured chain-of-thought, so oversight will be needed on internal representations such as this.

# Title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function

Authors: Tiansheng Huang , Ananth Balashankar , Virat Shejwalkar , Santosh Pande , Ling Liu
View a PDF of the paper titled Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function, by Tiansheng Huang and 4 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks. To mitigate harmful agentic RL, we propose Bait, a defense that mitigates the attack via proactively probing the reward function. Experimental results show that such a simple defense can sufficiently mitigate learning from a harmful reward function and can still learn from a benign reward function that promotes benign agentic tasks. Further analysis on both empirical and theoretical aspects shows that an adaptive attacker who assumes the knowledge of Bait defense cannot perfectly subvert it due to a systematic challenge. Source code is available at this https URL .

# Title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation

Authors: Eve Fleisig , Joachim Baumann , Dylan Hadfield-Menell , Dirk Hovy
View a PDF of the paper titled Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation, by Eve Fleisig and 3 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

# Title: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs

Authors: Tim De Wachter , Kyryl Volkov , Myrto Eleftheria Gkogkou , Mathieu Huysman
View a PDF of the paper titled Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs, by Tim De Wachter and 3 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: We ask whether small, open-weight decision models can support vulnerability discovery in open-source software at scale and what the surrounding system must provide. These models answer a typed question in one forward pass, returning scores for the permitted answers rather than text. Our harness selects widely packaged C and C++ projects and uses deterministic incomplete-fix miners and shape localizers to decide where to look. Intern-Decision-4B, a 4B-parameter open-weight decision model, then scores every candidate function. The scores rank the queues rather than accept or reject candidates, apart from a low reach-score floor that some queues kept. The search uses no frontier model.

Alone, the model is weak: it separates vulnerable from benign functions with AUC 0.73, but a vulnerable function from its own patch with only 0.56. It is more useful for ordering candidates. On 75 public CVEs from projects without any of our findings, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, 1.4 times as often as under random order of the same queues. Recall is bounded mainly by where the localizers look. On the campaign's own queues the model's order placed 7.5 times more confirmed findings in the top 10 than random order, an observed, selection-biased upper bound. On three GB10 systems, the harness searched more than 4,000 projects at 900-1,100 repositories per hour. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings; by worst-case CVSS v3.1, 12 are critical,

# Title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting

Authors: Dustin Rubin , Vincenzo Timmel , Xufeng He , Aritra Saha , JooMan Kim , Vijay Madisetti
View a PDF of the paper titled A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting, by Dustin Rubin and 5 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo~3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3\% accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1\%). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1\% and 89.6\%, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. # Title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents

Authors: Charles Xiao
View a PDF of the paper titled When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents, by Charles Xiao

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. We develop controlled counterfactual task variants that vary risk content, source provenance, and warning wording, and evaluate a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs, caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from $9.8\%$ to $86.3\%$, despite unchanged clean-task completion. Matched wording comparisons further reveal sensitivity to warning language, with substantial variation across models and environments. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, while forgery and sensitive-content controls expose its dependence on authoritative evidence and its limitations in preserving confidentiality. These results motivate evaluating agent safety through the justification for restraint, alongside the safety of actions taken.

The search turned up one important correction: the HMICFRS report on wrongful arrests covers retrospective facial recognition, not live facial recognition. The live FR element of your query isn't addressed by it.

**What the report covers:** The inspection was commissioned by the Home Secretary and examined retrospective facial recognition (RFR) by police forces and the National Crime Agency. The report did not examine live facial recognition or operator-initiated facial recognition. Coverage of the live FR side comes from separate government proposals. One report notes that the Home Secretary is proposing to introduce a new law to limit the deployment to identify "wanted" criminals and registered sex offenders at fixed times, with the public alerted to their live operation.
